entries.title: The ezafe
entries.summary: Put -e between a noun and the word that describes or owns it: ketāb-e man, my book.

blocks.heading: What it does
blocks.body: Dari links two words that belong together with a short -e sound. It joins a noun to the adjective that describes it, or to the person or thing that owns it. English puts the describing word first (a new book). Dari puts the noun first and links the rest to it: ketāb-e naw, literally 'book-of new'.

blocks.heading: You hear it, you don't see it
blocks.body: The -e is usually not written in Dari script. کتاب من is read ketāb-e man, even though nothing between the two words shows it. The transliteration line always shows it, so use that line to learn where it goes.
After -ā, -ō or -ū the ezafe is written as ی: هوای کابل. After -a, and after -ī, it is usually left unwritten, just like after a consonant: خانه ما.

blocks.heading: Chains
blocks.body: You can keep linking: noun, then adjective, then owner, each joined with -e. The last word of the chain takes nothing.

items.en: The weather in Kabul is cold.

blocks.why: The owner comes after the thing, never before it. man ketāb sounds like 'I, book'.
Adjectives follow the noun in Dari. Put the noun first and link the adjective with -e.

blocks.heading: A shorter way to say 'my'
blocks.body: For 'my', 'your' and 'his' or 'her' you will often see an ending on the noun instead of a separate word: کتابم, ketābam, my book. Both are correct. See Possessive endings.

entries.title: Present tense with mē-
entries.summary: mē- + present stem + ending: mēkhānam, I read. One pattern for almost every verb.

blocks.heading: One tense, two English meanings
blocks.body: Dari uses one present tense where English uses two. من نان می‌خورم means both 'I eat bread' and 'I am eating bread'. The rest of the sentence tells you which.

blocks.heading: Learn the stem with the verb

blocks.body: The present stem often looks different from the infinitive, so there is no safe way to guess it. Learn it together with the verb.

items.target: من هر روز به مکتب می‌روم
items.translit: man har rōz ba maktab mērawam
items.en: I go to school every day.

blocks.heading: Saying 'don't'
blocks.body: Change mē- to namē-. Everything else stays the same.

blocks.why: dāshtan, 'to have', takes no mē- in the present. The same goes for 'to be': hastam, never mēhastam.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: Kabul speech shortens the most common verbs: mērawam becomes mērum. man becomes ma, and ba before a place is often left out. You will see this spelling in messages and on social media.

entries.title: The object marker rā
entries.summary: Put rā after a specific object: ketāb rā mēkhānam, I read the book.

blocks.heading: What rā marks
blocks.body: rā comes right after the object of the verb when that object is specific: a thing you both have in mind, a named person, or something with 'this' or 'my'. It is how Dari tells 'I read the book' from 'I read books'.

blocks.heading: When to use it
rows: with this or that: īn khāna

blocks.body: With 'me' and 'you', rā joins the pronoun in writing: man + rā is مرا, marā, and tu + rā is ترا, turā.

blocks.heading: After the whole phrase
blocks.body: rā goes after the complete object, however long it is. It never breaks into an ezafe chain.

blocks.why: barādar-e man is one object, so rā waits until the end of it.

blocks.heading: Not for the subject
blocks.body: rā only ever marks the object. The person doing the action never takes it, and a place you go to takes ba, not rā.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: In speech and in casual writing rā is usually ra, spelled ره.

entries.title: Pronouns and 'to be'
entries.summary: Six pronouns, each with its own form of 'to be' at the end of the sentence: man shāgerd hastam, I am a student.

blocks.heading: Six pronouns
blocks.body: Dari has six personal pronouns. ō means both 'he' and 'she': Dari has no grammatical gender, so adjectives and verbs never change for male or female.

blocks.heading: Polite 'you'
blocks.body: Use shumā with anyone older than you, with strangers and with anyone you want to show respect to, even when you speak to one person. tu is for close friends, children and people your own age you know well.

blocks.why: 'To be' closes the sentence. The word that describes you comes before it.
The form of 'to be' has to match the person. ast is for one person or thing that is not 'I' or 'you': ō, īn (this), ketāb (the book).

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: In Kabul, man is said ma and hastam is said astum. People type it this way in messages too.

entries.title: Word order: the verb goes last
entries.summary: Who does it comes first, the verb comes last, and everything else goes in between.

blocks.heading: The basic order
blocks.body: A Dari sentence starts with who does something and ends with the verb. Time, place and the object all go in between.

items.target: من امروز در خانه نان می‌خورم
items.translit: man emrōz dar khāna nān mēkhuram
items.en: I am eating at home today.
He is going to Kabul tomorrow.

blocks.heading: Time can come first
blocks.body: Words like dīrōz (yesterday), emrōz (today) and fardā (tomorrow) often open the sentence, even before who. The verb still stays last.

items.en: Yesterday I went to the bazaar.

blocks.heading: You can drop the pronoun
blocks.body: The ending of the verb already says who: raftam can only mean 'I went'. So the pronoun is often left out.

items.en: Yesterday I went to the bazaar.

blocks.heading: Small words and describing words
blocks.body: One thing works like English: prepositions such as dar (in) and ba (to) go before their noun. One thing does not: adjectives follow the noun, joined with the ezafe.

blocks.why: The object goes before the verb, not after it as in English.

entries.title: Plurals: -hā and -ān
entries.summary: Add -hā to make almost any noun plural: ketāb, ketāb-hā. After a number the noun stays singular.

blocks.heading: -hā works for everything
blocks.body: Add -hā to the end of a noun. It works for things, animals and people. In Dari script it is joined with a half-space, so the word stays readable: کتاب‌ها.

blocks.heading: -ān for people
blocks.body: Nouns for people can also take -ān. It sounds more formal and is common in writing, but -hā is always understood.

blocks.heading: After a number, no plural
blocks.body: A number already says how many, so the noun after it stays singular: dū ketāb, literally 'two book'.

blocks.why: After a number the noun never takes -hā.

blocks.heading: Plural with the ezafe
blocks.body: A -hā plural ends in a vowel, so its ezafe is -ye and is written ی: ketāb-hā-ye man, my books. An -ān plural ends in a consonant and takes a plain -e: dōstān-e man, my friends.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: In Kabul speech -hā usually loses its h and becomes -ā. You will see it spelled that way in messages.

entries.title: Asking questions
entries.summary: Put the question word where the answer would go and keep the verb last. For yes or no, just let your voice rise.

blocks.heading: Same order as the answer
blocks.body: Dari does not move words around to ask a question. The question word sits exactly where the answer would sit, and the verb stays at the end.
The letters کی spell kī, who. They can also spell kay, when, but in Kabul 'when' is usually said che waqt.

items.en: How many brothers do you have?

blocks.heading: chīst: what is
blocks.body: 'What is' is squeezed into one word, chīst: nām-e shumā chīst? What is your name?

blocks.heading: Yes or no questions
blocks.body: Keep the sentence exactly as it is and let your voice rise at the end. In writing, add the Dari question mark ؟. Formal Dari can open with āyā, but you rarely need it. Answer with balē (yes) or na (no).

blocks.why: Dari never moves the verb to the front to make a question. Only your voice changes.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: Kabul's everyday 'How are you?' to a friend drops hāl and uses astī, the spoken form of hastī.

entries.title: Saying no: na- and nēst
entries.summary: Put na- in front of the verb: mērawam, namērawam. 'To be' has its own negative: nēstam, I am not.

blocks.heading: One prefix
blocks.body: To make almost any verb negative, put na- in front of it. In the present tense mē- becomes namē-.

items.en: He didn't go to school yesterday.

blocks.heading: Answering no
blocks.body: On its own, 'no' is na, نه, and 'yes' is balē, بلی.

blocks.why: na- joins the verb as a prefix. Written as a separate word, نه is an answer, 'no'.
'To be' does not take na-. Use its own negative forms: nēstam, nēst.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: In speech the final t of nēst is usually dropped: nēs. Messages often spell it that way.

entries.title: Possessive endings
entries.summary: Instead of ketāb-e man you can add an ending to the noun: ketābam, my book. Both are correct.

blocks.heading: A shorter 'my'
blocks.body: Dari has two ways to say whose something is. The long way links a pronoun with the ezafe: ketāb-e man. The short way adds an ending to the noun: ketābam. They mean the same; the short way is what you hear most in speech.

blocks.heading: After -a
blocks.body: After a noun ending in -a, the ending is written apart with a half-space. The singular endings keep their vowel, the plural ones lose their e: khāna-am, my house, but khāna-mān, our house.

blocks.heading: With an adjective
blocks.body: The ending goes on the last word of the whole phrase. With an adjective, that is the adjective: barādar-e kalānam, my older brother.

blocks.why: The ending waits until the end of the phrase, after the adjective.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: The spelling is the same, but in Kabul the endings are said -et and -esh: ketābet, ketābesh.

entries.title: Prepositions: dar, ba, az, bā
entries.summary: Small words that go before a noun: dar kābul (in Kabul), ba maktab (to school), az khāna (from home), bā dōst (with a friend).

blocks.heading: Before the noun
blocks.body: Prepositions work like English ones: they come right before the noun they belong to.

items.en: He is going to the bazaar.

blocks.heading: ba or dar?
blocks.body: ba is for moving towards a place. For being in a place, use dar.

blocks.why: You are not moving, so the place takes dar, not ba.

blocks.heading: Some take the ezafe
blocks.body: A few words that began life as nouns link to their noun with the ezafe: pusht-e khāna, behind the house; zēr-e mēz, under the table. pēsh-e works the same way and usually means 'at someone's place': pēsh-e dāktar, at the doctor's. barā-ye already carries its ezafe.

blocks.why: Prepositions go before the noun. Only the verb moves to the end of the sentence.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: In Kabul speech dar becomes da, usually typed ده, and da is also used where writing has ba: ma da maktab mērum, I go to school.

entries.title: 'There is' and 'to have'
entries.summary: hast says something exists: chāy hast, there is tea. dāram says you have it: chāy dāram, I have tea.

blocks.heading: ast or hast?
blocks.body: For 'it' or 'he' and 'she', Dari has two words. ast links a thing to a description: the tea is hot. hast says that something exists: there is tea. The negative of both is nēst. With every other person there is just one set, hastam, hastī and so on, as on the 'to be' page.

items.en: There is no water in the room.

blocks.heading: To have: dāshtan
blocks.body: When dāshtan means 'to have', it takes no mē- in the present: dāram, not mēdāram. Its negative is nadāram. The same goes for dōst dāram, 'I like'.

blocks.why: hast says a thing exists somewhere. It cannot mean 'I have'. For having, use dāram.

entries.title: Simple past
entries.summary: Take the infinitive, drop -an and add the endings: raftan, raftam, I went.

blocks.heading: Built from the infinitive
blocks.body: Every past form starts from the past stem, which is the infinitive without its final -an: raftan → raft, kardan → kard, khurdan → khurd.
ō takes no ending at all: ō raft, he went. And unlike the present, the simple past has no mē-.

items.en: Yesterday I went to the bazaar.

blocks.heading: Didn't
blocks.body: Put na- in front: naraftam, I didn't go.

right.en: Yesterday I went to the bazaar.

blocks.why: A time word like dīrōz does not make the sentence past. The verb itself has to be in the past.
The ending must match the person, and for ō there is no ending.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: The spelling stays the same, but Kabul speech says the ending -am as -um: raftum, kardum.

entries.title: Comparing: -tar and -tarīn
entries.summary: Add -tar for 'more': kalāntar az, bigger than. Add -tarīn for 'most' and put it before the noun: kalāntarīn shahr, the biggest city.

blocks.heading: More: -tar
blocks.body: To say 'bigger' or 'newer', add -tar to the adjective. The thing you compare with comes after az, which here means 'than'. In careful writing it is joined with a half-space, کلان‌تر, but you will often see it written joined, کلانتر.

items.target: کابل از شهر ما کلان‌تر است
items.translit: kābul az shahr-e mā kalāntar ast
items.en: Kabul is bigger than our city.

blocks.heading: Most: -tarīn
blocks.body: Add -tarīn for 'the most'. Unlike ordinary adjectives, it comes before the noun, with no ezafe.

blocks.heading: Than all of them
blocks.body: Everyday Dari also says 'the most' with az hama, 'than all': az hama kalāntar, the biggest of all.

items.target: این خانه از همه کلان‌تر است
items.translit: īn khāna az hama kalāntar ast
items.en: This house is the biggest of all.

blocks.why: -tarīn words go before the noun and take no ezafe. Only -tar and plain adjectives follow the noun.

entries.title: Talking about the future
entries.summary: In everyday Dari the present tense plus a time word is the future: fardā mērawam, I'll go tomorrow. Writing also has khāham raft.

blocks.heading: Everyday: just the present
blocks.body: For plans and predictions, Dari simply uses the present tense. A time word like fardā (tomorrow) makes it future.

blocks.heading: Written: khāham + past stem
blocks.body: News, books and formal speech use a separate future: the present of khāstan without mē-, followed by the bare past stem of the verb.

items.target: او فردا به کابل خواهد رفت
items.translit: ō fardā ba kābul khāhad raft
items.en: He will go to Kabul tomorrow.

blocks.heading: Not, and compounds
blocks.body: Put na- on khāham: nakhāham raft, I will not go. With a compound verb, khāham sits between the two parts: kār khāham kard.

blocks.why: Only khāham changes for the person. The second verb is always the bare past stem, with no ending.
With mē-, khāham means 'I want'. The future uses it bare.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: In Kabul 'tomorrow' is usually sabā, ba before a place is often left out, and the future is simply the present: mērum.

entries.title: Past and present stems
entries.summary: Every verb has two stems. The past stem (raft) builds the past tenses; the present stem (raw) builds the present, commands and 'want to' forms.

blocks.heading: Two stems per verb
blocks.body: A Dari verb is listed by its infinitive, ending in -an: raftan, to go. Every other form is built from one of its two stems, so learning a verb means learning both.

blocks.heading: The past stem is easy
blocks.body: The past stem is always the infinitive without -an: raftan → raft, kardan → kard. No exceptions.

blocks.heading: The present stem must be learned
blocks.body: The present stem often looks different and cannot be guessed. Most verbs in -īdan are the kind exception: drop the whole -īdan. kharīdan → khar, fahmīdan → fahm, pursīdan → purs. Two common ones do not follow it: dīdan → bīn and shunīdan → shunaw.

items.en: I write a letter every day.

blocks.why: The present is built on the present stem, nawīs, not on the past stem. mēnawishtam means 'I used to write'.

entries.title: Commands with bu-
entries.summary: Put bu- on the present stem to tell someone to do something: bukhur, eat! Add -ēd to be polite: lutfan bukhurēd.

blocks.heading: The command form
blocks.body: A command is the prefix bu- plus the present stem, with no ending. It is how you speak to one person you know well. The prefix is written ب and its vowel is not written. In Afghanistan it is usually said bu-: bukhur, bukun, buraw, bubīn. Some speakers say bi-, and before yā it is always bi-: biyā.

blocks.heading: Polite: add -ēd
blocks.body: To one person you respect, or to several people, add -ēd. Starting with lutfan (please) makes it a polite request.

blocks.heading: Don't
blocks.body: For 'don't', na- replaces the bu- prefix: nakhur, don't eat; naraw, don't go.

blocks.heading: Compound verbs
blocks.body: Compound verbs keep the first part and put the command on kardan, usually without bu-: kār kun, work! kumak kunēd, help!

blocks.why: Commands never take mē-. They take bu-.

blocks.heading: Come!
blocks.body: āmadan, to come, has the stem ā. bu- + ā is written بیا and said biyā, come! To be polite: biyāyēd (بیایید).

entries.title: Want, can, must
entries.summary: mēkhāham, mētawānam and bāyad are followed by a second verb with bu-: mēkhāham burawam, I want to go.

blocks.heading: Two verbs, both with an ending
blocks.body: English says 'I want to go' with an infinitive. Dari uses two finished verbs instead: 'I want' + '(that) I go'. The second verb takes bu- (written ب) and a normal ending. This is called the subjunctive.

blocks.heading: bāyad stays the same
blocks.body: bāyad never changes: the same word for every person. Only the second verb shows who.

blocks.heading: Compound verbs
blocks.body: Compound verbs usually drop bu- in this form: kār kunam rather than kār bukunam.

blocks.heading: Not
blocks.body: Put the negative on the first verb: namēkhāham burawam, I don't want to go. With bāyad, nabāyad means 'must not'.

blocks.why: The second verb is never in the present with mē-. It takes bu-.
The English-style infinitive does not work here. Give the second verb its own ending.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: Kabul speech shortens mētawānam to mētānum and burawam to burum.

entries.title: Compound verbs: kār kardan
entries.summary: Many Dari verbs are a noun plus a helper verb: kār kardan, to work. Only the helper changes: kār mēkunam, kār nakardam.

blocks.heading: Meaning plus helper
blocks.body: A large share of Dari verbs are built from a noun or adjective and a small helper verb, most often kardan (to do). The first part carries the meaning; the helper carries the tense and the person.

blocks.heading: Only the helper changes
blocks.body: mē-, na- and the ending all go on the helper. The first part stays in front and does not change. Only khāham, in the formal future, can come between them: kār khāham kard.

blocks.heading: kardan or shudan?
blocks.body: kardan means 'to do' something, shudan means 'to become'. The pair often gives an active and a non-active verb: kharāb kardan, to break something; kharāb shudan, to break down. khush shudan means 'to be pleased'.

blocks.why: mē- belongs to the helper verb, not to the noun in front of it.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: suhbat kardan is the more formal word for 'talking'. In everyday Dari people say gap zadan, and it is fine in writing too. Kabul speech then shortens the verb: gap mēzanēm.

entries.title: Past continuous: mēraftam
entries.summary: Put mē- on the simple past for 'used to' or 'was doing': mēraftam, I used to go, or I was going.

blocks.heading: One form, two meanings
blocks.body: Add mē- to a simple past verb. The result covers two English meanings: a habit in the past ('I used to go') and something that was going on at the time ('I was going').

items.en: I used to go to school every day.
We used to live in Kabul.

blocks.heading: Watch the spelling
blocks.body: For 'he' and 'she' this form can look exactly like the present: می‌خورد is both mēkhurad, he eats, and mēkhurd, he used to eat. Only the context and the pronunciation tell them apart.

items.en: He always used to drink tea.

blocks.heading: Not
blocks.body: Put na- in front of mē-, just as in the present: namēraftam, I didn't use to go.

right.en: I used to go to school every day.

blocks.why: 'Every day' in the past is a habit, so the verb needs mē-. Without it, raftam sounds like one finished action, not a habit.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: Kabul speech says the ending -um, and messages usually skip the half-space: میرفتم.

entries.title: Present perfect: rafta-am
entries.summary: Past stem + -a, then a short ending: rafta-am, I have gone. For 'he' or 'she' it is rafta ast.

blocks.heading: When to use it
blocks.body: Use it for experiences ('I have been to Kabul') and for results that still matter now ('he has eaten'). It is also often used for things you heard about or worked out rather than saw. That is why the news writes gufta ast, '(he) has said', for what someone said.

blocks.heading: In script
blocks.body: The -a is written ه, and the endings join it with a half-space: رفته‌ام. Only 'he' or 'she' keeps ast as a separate word.

blocks.heading: Not yet
blocks.body: na- goes on the front: narafta-am, I haven't gone. With hanōz (yet) it means 'not yet'.

blocks.why: The perfect is built on the -a form, rafta, not on the simple past raftam.

entries.title: 'A' and 'some': yak and -ē
entries.summary: Say 'a book' with yak ketāb or with the ending -ē: ketābē. Either is enough, but you will also hear both together: yak rōzē, one day.

blocks.heading: Two ways to say 'a'
blocks.body: Dari has no word for 'the': a plain noun is already definite or general. For 'a', put yak (one) before the noun, or add -ē to its end. Either is enough; yak is more usual in speech, and the two also appear together: yak rōzē, one day.

blocks.heading: With an adjective
blocks.body: With an adjective, -ē moves to the end of the phrase: ketāb-e nawē, a new book.

blocks.heading: Someone, something
blocks.body: Some everyday words are built this way: kasē, someone; chīzē, something; jāyē, somewhere.

blocks.why: yak means 'one', so it cannot go with a plural. For 'some books', use chand (a few).

entries.title: Writing: the half-space
entries.summary: Dari joins some word parts with a half-space, a break between letters without a gap: می‌خوانم, کتاب‌ها.

blocks.heading: What it is
blocks.body: Arabic-script letters join to their neighbours. A half-space stops that join without leaving a gap, so a prefix or ending stays visibly separate but still part of the word.

blocks.why: In careful writing mē- is kept apart with a half-space. Written together (میخوانم) is common in quick typing, as below, but not in edited text.
A full space splits one word into two. mē- is a prefix, not a word.

blocks.heading: On a phone
blocks.body: On a computer with the Persian (Standard) layout, Shift+Space types a half-space. On an Android phone, hold the space bar. In quick messages many people skip it and type میخوانم; you will need to read both.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: Casual Kabuli messages rarely use the half-space, partly because spoken forms like کتابا and میرم do not need one.
